senses: Supporting slavery.
examples: By 1835 the excitement was at its height, and especially along the line of the moral and religious argumentation, where the proslavery men met talk with talk.

His proslavery views were shaped not only by money and status but also by his deeply racist views, which he tried to justify through pseudoscience.

senses: Any process of writing involving the use of heat.
examples: Thermography, which imitates engraving, costs far less because it employs no dies or plates.

senses: Either of the two orifices located on the nose (or on the beak of a bird); used as a passage for air and other gases to travel the nasal passages.
ety: From Middle English nostrille, from Old English nosþyrel. Compare Old Frisian nosterle (“nostril”), modern West Frisian noaster (“nostrill”). Compare also Middle Low German noster (“nostril”), from Proto-Germanic *nustriz (“nostril”). By surface analysis, nose + thirl (“hole”).

senses: Affected by a fever; feverish.
Heated; impassioned; enthusiastic to the point of distraction.
examples: Amid all the fevered anticipation of this fixture, few would have expected to witness an aesthetically pleasing example of the beautiful game.
To rephrase in less fevered rhetoric, a regional alliance might take shape independent of the U.S.

senses: A bunch or part projecting like the hip.
ety: From huck (from Middle English hoke (“hook”), hokebone, probably so called because of its round shape) + -le. See also hook.

senses: A type of hunting dog from Russia.
examples: Q—The Russians picked a laika to occupy the space capsule. Do you think a dachshund would have been a wiser choice?
Indeed, they have been hybridising for a very long time, as is evidenced by the laika, a wolf-like dog that even today accompanies various Siberian peoples.

senses: caviar from the albino beluga
Submersed or dissolved in, or obtained with the use of methanol.
examples: The catalyst solution (0.5M methanolic sodium methoxide) is made by dissolving dry sodium in anhydrous methanol and is stable for several months.
In the case Anabaena fertilissima only two extracts i.e. methanolic and ethyl acetate extracts were found active as compared to previously studied Anabaena variabilis.

senses: A Mexican dish consisting of beef tongue used to make tacos.
ety: Borrowed from Spanish lengua (“tongue”). Doublet of langue, lingua, and tongue.

senses: A unit of volume or capacity equivalent to 100 litres. Symbol: hL
ety: From French hectolitre. By surface analysis, hecto- + litre.

senses: To flog with a cowhide.
An animal without vertebrae (i.e., without a backbone).
A spineless person; a coward.
The transmission of radio or television channels from the broadcaster into the networks that deliver them to the audience.
coloured bay, reddish brown, notably said of equines
ety: From French bayard, from Middle French bayard, from Old French béart, bayart, baiart, boieart, boyart, bayard (“stretcher”), of uncertain origin. By surface analysis, bay + -ard.

senses: Someone or something that twitches.
ety: From twitch + -er. The birdwatching sense first recorded in 1970 and recalled as being in use in 1968; claimed by R.E. Emmett to have arisen in 1950s Britain in reference to birder Howard Medhurst who often arrived at rare‑bird sites shivering after riding pillion on Emmett's motorcycle.

senses: An instance thereof.
ety: Borrowed from French refoulement (“act of pushing something back (as gunpowder into a gun barrel, or water by a dam); act of water overflowing; forced relocation of a group of people; forced repatriation of asylum-seekers or refugees”), from refouler (“to cause to flow or turn back; to repress, suppress; to repulse; to trample on again”) (from re- (prefix meaning ‘again’) + fouler (“to impress, stamp; to trample, walk on; to mistreat, oppress”) (ultimately from Medieval Latin fullare (“to make cloth denser and firmer by soaking, beating and pressing, to full”), from Latin fullō (“one who fulls

senses: A toxic extract of certain false hellebores (Veratrum album or Veratrum viride), formerly used as a pesticide.
ety: From Middle English ellebore, from Old French ellebre, elebore, from Medieval Latin eleborus, via Latin from Ancient Greek ἑλλέβορος (helléboros), possibly from ἄλκη (álkē, “elk [moose]”) βιβρώσκω (bibrṓskō, “to eat”). The initial h was restored in English to reflect the Ancient Greek etymology.

senses: Free; liberal; loose.
Relaxed; hence, cheerful, merry.
Able to be dissolved; soluble.
ety: Borrowed from Latin solutus, past participle of solvo.

senses: The excrement of a cow.
ety: From Middle English cowedong, kowe donge; equivalent to cow + dung.
examples: The walls, which are fixed direct into the ground without a plinth, are made of wattle and plastered with a thin lair of mud or cowdung.

senses: Synonym of by-election.
examples: This was perhaps her expression of gratitude for the GJMM on the latter's support for the Trinamool candidate in the Rajgunj assembly bypoll.
Yet the ruling party has been able to win the Howrah bypoll comfortably.
Sawant is the widow of former MLA Bala Sawant who died sometime back and due to this this bypoll was held.

senses: A Fresnel lens or a light feature using such a lens
Characteristic of, or causing one to vomit.
examples: Their communications from the peace talks are vomitous torrents of insult and threat.

senses: The proprietor of a hotel or restaurant; an innkeeper.
ety: After Boniface, the innkeeper in George Farquhar's 1707 comedic play The Beaux' Stratagem.

senses: Having blisters.
The boundary between the Earth's magnetosphere and the sun's plasma.
A group of five, particularly (music) a tuplet of five notes to be played in the time for four.
One of a group of five, particularly babies born from the same mother during the same birth.
A cycle adapted for five riders, all of whom can assist in the propulsion.
ety: From quintuple + -et, from Middle French quintuple.

senses: A fun person.
The act or art of declaiming; rhetorical delivery; loud speaking in public.
The public recitation of speeches as an exercise in schools and colleges.
A set or harangue; declamatory discourse.
Pretentious rhetorical display, with more sound than sense.
ety: From French déclamation, from Latin dēclāmātiō, dēclāmātiōnem, from dēclāmō, dēclāmāre; see declaim.

senses: Having locks or tufts.
Secured with a padlock.
examples: Sidonia's answer was that she had enclosed the spell in a padlocked box and flung it into the sea.
Both halves feature lyrics that are so teen-girly they sound like they were written in pink ink in a padlocked diary with hearts and frowny faces for punctuation.

senses: A person or organization employed in fracking.
examples: Conoco on Monday announced a $9.7 billion all-stock takeover of Concho Resources (CXO), a fracker squarely focused on the Permian Basin, the massive West Texas oilfield at the heart of the shale revolution.

senses: A demonstration of affection and well-wishing to someone leaving a place or group to begin a new undertaking; a farewell.
A party for an colleague who is leaving; a farewell party.
A memorial service or funeral.
examples: We had a sendoff for our departing colleague as he left for a new job.

senses: One who or that which trills.
A musical ornament consisting of a rapid alternation between two adjacent notes.
examples: When the left hand is the triller, it might seem more difficult to stabilize with the right, which is mostly off the flute.

senses: The condition of being a spinster.
The time during which one is a spinster.
A film featuring a particular movie star.
Something meriting a rating of the specified number of stars.
examples: The Central Board of Film Certification (CBFC) has refused to certify Nawazuddin Siddiqui starrer 'Haraamkhor' objecting to its theme which deals with a student-teacher romance.

senses: One who conceptualizes, designs, builds, programs, and experiments with robots.
ety: Coined by Isaac Asimov in 1940. robot + -ic + -ist. Coined in his short story "Robbie" (initially published under the title "Strange Playfellow").
examples: Johnson is an expert Roboticist.

senses: A small box or container to hold snuff or loose tobacco.
examples: He held out his snuffbox of old gold, with a great amethyst in the centre of the lid.

senses: A person who creates cocktails, especially one considered an artist in that craft.
Any bartender.
A disc jockey.
A title of bishops in their role as ordinaries (arbiters of canon law) over their respective dioceses.
ety: From Medieval Latin hierarcha, from Ancient Greek ἱεράρχης (hierárkhēs) Derived from ἱερός (hierós, “holy”) + -άρχης (-árkhēs, “ruler”, “leader”). ἱερός from Proto-Hellenic *iherós, from Proto-Indo-European *ish₁ros. There are a number of candidate cognates with this word. Compare Sanskrit इषिर (iṣira, “vigorous, fresh, blooming”) and Oscan 𐌀𐌉𐌔𐌖𐌔𐌉𐌔 (aisusis).

senses: A small, mischievous humanoid creature in Iberian (Spanish/Portuguese), Latin American, and Philippine folklore/mythology; an imp.
Heightened inspiration or passion, especially in flamenco.
Personal charm.
ety: Borrowed from Spanish duende and (especially in reference to Portuguese or Brazilian folklore) Portuguese duende. Doublet of duwende.
examples: For quotations using this term, see Citations:duende.
The duende is a momentary burst of inspiration, the blush of all that is truly alive, all that the performer is creating at a certain moment.
